First, we need to find the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x),$ which is the solution to the homogeneous equation

$$
{y}^{″}-{y}^{′}-2y=0.
$$

Writing down and solving the auxiliary equation gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}-\lambda -2 & =0 \\ (\lambda +1)(\lambda -2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So $\lambda =-1$ or $\lambda =2$, and therefore the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{c}(x)=A{e}^{-x}+B{e}^{2x}.
$$

We now need to find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x).$

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is $3\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡x.$ Therefore, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}=\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡x,
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =-\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡x+\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ {y}^{″} & =-\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡x-\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute the derivatives into the differential equation:

$$
-\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡x-\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡x-(-\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡x+\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡x)-2(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡x)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡x
$$

Grouping the terms on the left-hand side gives:

$$
(-3\alpha -\beta )\operatorname{cos}⁡x+(\alpha -3\beta )\operatorname{sin}⁡x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡x
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}-3\alpha -\beta =3\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡x) \\ \alpha -3\beta =-1\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =-1,$ $\beta =0.$

Therefore, the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=-\operatorname{cos}⁡x.
$$

The general solution is given by

$$
y(x)={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x),
$$

and therefore, the general solution in our case is

$$
y=A{e}^{-x}+B{e}^{2x}-\operatorname{cos}⁡x.
$$

Now let us find constants $A$ and $B.$ 

Substituting $y(0)=0$ into the general solution gives

$$
A+B-1=0.
$$

We now need to apply the condition ${y}^{′}(0)=-1.$ First, we differentiate $y$ to find ${y}^{′}$:

$$
{y}^{′}=-A{e}^{-x}+2B{e}^{2x}+\operatorname{sin}⁡x
$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(0)=-1$ into the above gives

$$
-A+2B=-1.
$$

Therefore, we have the following system of equations for $A$ and $B$:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}A+B=1 \\ -A+2B=-1\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $A=1,$ $B=0.$
Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y={e}^{-x}-\operatorname{cos}⁡x.
$$
